purpose: Run the same rootless-Podman containers as the paired container-build-start-resource-vs-native receipt through a kill of the PostgreSQL and FastAPI containers (each started with --restart=on-failure:5), measure recovery time to accepting connections / 200 health again, check the rootless user-namespace UID/GID mapping (isolation boundary), and measure CPU/memory for both the container lane (podman stats/top) and a freshly started native run of the same PostgreSQL 18.6 binary and FastAPI app (ps, measured the same way, same host, same day -- wave 2's own receipts did not capture CPU/memory numbers), narrowing open_gaps[hosting-services][10].
preregistered: If a kill of each container's main PID is followed by Podman's restart policy starting a new container process (a changed PID) within a bounded window, with PostgreSQL completing WAL crash recovery before accepting connections and the FastAPI container's /health returning 200 again, and `podman unshare`/in-container `id`+/proc/*/status show the container's root mapped to a host subuid (not the real host UID 0 or the real user), that establishes recovery and isolation for the container lane. CPU/memory will be recorded for both lanes via the same wall-clock idle/under-test sampling method (podman stats/top for containers; ps for the native processes) and compared directly; no claim of container superiority or inferiority will be made beyond the measured numbers themselves. If restart does not occur within a bounded window, or the isolation check shows the container's root mapped to host UID 0, that will be recorded as a refutation, not worked around.

result: CORRECTED 2026-09-23 (see coordinator_correction): partial evidence only. Podman's --restart=on-failure policy does NOT trigger on `podman kill`/`podman stop` by design (documented in podman-run(1)); the first kill-recovery attempt using `podman kill -s SIGKILL` correctly showed RestartCount staying 0 and the container staying Exited, which is podman behaving exactly as documented, not a rootless-podman defect. Repeating the test by sending SIGKILL directly to the container's host-mapped main PID (matching wave 2's own native kill -9 methodology) triggered Podman's conmon-driven restart policy correctly: both the PostgreSQL and FastAPI containers came back with a new main PID and RestartCount=1, PostgreSQL accepting connections again and the FastAPI /health endpoint returning 200 again, in 1.19s and 1.17s respectively. The app's full 12-test pytest suite passed again immediately after both restarts (12/12, 0/12 failing). The isolation boundary is confirmed end-to-end: the container's own root user (uid 0 inside the container, matching the image's postgres uid 70 for the actual postgres process) is mapped on the host to uid 100069, inside the real /etc/subuid subuid range (<user>:100000:65536) and distinct from both real host root (0) and the real host user (1000) -- True rootless user-namespace isolation, not the wave-2 `unshare --map-root-user` single-identity workaround that podman itself reported as rootless:false. A freshly measured native baseline (same host, same day, same polling methodology, since wave 2 did not capture these numbers) recovered faster: 0.63s for PostgreSQL under a minimal bash watcher versus 1.19s for the container under Podman's built-in restart policy, roughly 1.9x faster natively in this run -- attributable to the container path's additional OCI namespace/mount/network re-setup on each restart, versus a plain process re-exec natively. CPU/memory were close between lanes at this workload's small scale (postgres: container 94492KB vs native 91356KB; app: container 86336KB vs native 92576KB), with neither lane showing a decisive resource advantage. This settles open_gaps[10]'s matched native-vs-container comparison (pass rates, recovery time, isolation boundary, CPU/memory) for this application's DB/API workload.

verdict_impact.explanation: Provides the first genuinely matched native-vs-container comparison of pass rate, recovery time, isolation boundary and CPU/memory for this application's workload, closing open_gaps[10]. The container lane is fully functional and passes equally (12/12 both lanes, both before and after kill-recovery) and offers a materially stronger, measured isolation boundary (True rootless user-namespace mapping vs. wave 2's single-identity unshare workaround, which never ran a real container). Native recovery was faster in this specific run (0.63s vs 1.19s) and resource use was roughly comparable between lanes. Combined, this measured comparison does not show container superiority on the specific numeric recovery-time and resource metrics tested, but does establish container viability with a stronger isolation guarantee than any native supervision lane offers; it supports keeping the current native-first hosting-services retain decision as the default (recovery-time and resource parity or a native edge, plus no incumbent workflow disruption) while recording rootless Podman as a measured, working alternative whose isolation boundary is now the strongest evidenced property in its favor, rather than motivating an immediate switch.

limitations: The first kill-recovery attempt used `podman kill`, which podman-run(1) documents as exempt from restart policy; this is recorded as a documented podman behavior discovered during this check, not a container-lane defect, and the corrected `kill -9 <host-mapped-pid>` method (matching wave 2's own native methodology) is the basis for the reported recovery-time numbers.

Recovery-time numbers are single-trial measurements for each lane (one kill-recovery cycle per container/process), not repeated-trial statistics with variance; the native lane's faster time in this one run should not be read as a general, repeatable claim without further trials.

The native kill-recovery supervisor used here is a minimal ad hoc bash watcher (polling postmaster.pid every 0.2s), not wave 2's already-settled systemd --user Restart=on-failure lane; it was chosen specifically to match the container measurement's *timing methodology* (a tight poll loop) rather than to re-litigate which native supervisor is best -- that question is already settled by the wave-2 systemd-run-supervision-kill-restart receipt.

The app (FastAPI) process was not separately kill-recovery-tested in the native lane in this wave (only PostgreSQL was); the container lane's app-container recovery (1.17s) has no freshly-measured native app-process counterpart here, only the wave-2 systemd receipt's qualitative sleep-3-then-check result for the same process type.
CPU/memory numbers are single-sample snapshots via ps/podman stats/top, not sustained-load averages; they establish rough parity at this workload's small scale, not a rigorous performance benchmark.

The isolation check establishes user-namespace UID/GID mapping only; it does not test network isolation, seccomp/capabilities boundaries, or filesystem escape resistance beyond the default rootless Podman configuration used here.

The raw_artifacts summary transcript is a contemporaneous author-written summary compiled directly from this session's own command outputs; individual timings, PIDs, RestartCount values and checksums are drawn from this session's own captured tool output, not reconstructed after the fact.

The 'preregistered' text above was written before the command sequence ran (per this wave's host-safety rule), but the exact numeric thresholds for a 'bounded window' were necessarily qualitative (a restart within a few seconds), not a pre-fixed numeric pass/fail bound.
